reception.text: The Weekly People's Cause printed the full text of the Cinder Cone proclamation on its front page.
The Stockton Independent, reprinting the Oakland Tribune, wrongly guessed that the proclamation meant a cinder hill at the base of Mount Shasta in Siskiyou County.

legacy.text: Current USGS work dates Cinder Cone's eruptions to about 1650, restoring J. S. Diller's 1891 conclusion after R. H. Finch revived an 1851 date in 1937.
legacy.source: USGS Fact Sheet 023-00, How Old is "Cinder Cone"?

today.name: Lassen Volcanic National Park
today.note: The 1916 park act drew its boundary around the monument without mentioning it.

related.note: Signed the same day in nearly identical words, creating Lassen Peak National Monument.
Established the Lassen Peak Forest Reserve, out of which the monument was carved.

later_actions.text: Congress created Lassen Volcanic National Park, absorbing the monument.

reception.text: The Sacramento Daily Union and the Marysville Daily Appeal, reading the boundary map, placed the Lassen Peak monument in sections 34 and 35, T. 31 N., R. 4 E.
reception.source: Sacramento Daily Union, May 29, 1907, p. 16; Marysville Daily Appeal, May 31, 1907, p. 7

legacy.text: Lassen Peak began erupting on May 30, 1914; explosions on May 19 and May 22, 1915 created the Devastated Area and dropped ash as far as Elko, Nevada.
Benjamin Franklin Loomis's photographs of the eruptions brought national attention and supported the campaign for a national park.
The USGS ranks the Lassen volcanic center 11th of 161 U.S. volcanoes by threat and monitors it continuously.

today.name: Lassen Volcanic National Park
today.note: The park boundary takes in sections 34 and 35, where the monument lay.

related.note: Signed the same day in nearly identical words, creating Cinder Cone National Monument.
Established the Lassen Peak Forest Reserve, out of which the monument was carved.

later_actions.text: Congress created Lassen Volcanic National Park, absorbing the monument.

uncertain: How far the May 1915 flows ran down Lost Creek is not settled; USGS publications give conflicting distances.

reception.text: The first notice found was the Sacramento Daily Union's report that the proclamation had reached State Forester Lull, twenty-three days after signing.
Roughly a dozen and a half northern California papers covered the monuments through early June; the Feather River Bulletin printed the boundary map.
A syndicated paragraph about State Mineralogist Lewis E. Aubury receiving the proclamation was still running in small papers in November 1908.
reception.source: Newcastle News, June 19, 1907; Cloverdale Reveille, November 21, 1908

reception.text: Outside the Sacramento Valley the only notice found was a short paragraph in the San Francisco Call; nothing appeared east of the Sierra.

political_impact.text: Both monuments stayed under the Forest Service, which already managed the surrounding national forest.
political_impact.source: General Land Office, Commissioner's Annual Report, 1908, p. 19

political_impact.text: Signed during a congressional recess, the monuments drew no protest when Congress returned; the Congressional Record indexes for the 60th Congress have no entry for Lassen or Cinder Cone.
Because the monument route left timber and grazing untouched, no rancher, logger or miner lost anything and no lawsuit followed.

legacy.text: Representative John E. Raker's park bills began in 1912, before the eruptions, which revived his stalled effort.
legacy.source: National Park Service, Lassen Volcanic National Park administrative history

legacy.text: The 1916 park act absorbed both monuments without mentioning them, as Agriculture Secretary Wilson had predicted in 1907.
